The reproductive biology of Gadow's salamander (Pseudoeurycea gadovii) has been investigated through both field observations and controlled laboratory studies. Embryonic development proceeds within gelatinous egg masses deposited in cool, moist microhabitats, and eclosion occurs after a prolonged incubation period. When eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the age at birth is 110 days [ab = 110 days], a duration that reflects the relatively slow developmental rate characteristic of high-elevation plethodontids. Hatchlings emerge as fully formed, yolk-dependent larvae that initially rely on endogenous reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth is 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], a value derived from an egg diameter of approximately 3 millimeters, and this modest neonatal mass underscores the species' reliance on yolk provisioning during early life. Following yolk-sac resorption, the free-swimming tadpoles begin actively grazing on aquatic microorganisms, initiating a protracted larval period that can extend for many months under the cool thermal regimes typical of their montane habitat.

Metabolic measurements obtained through closed-system respirometry provide insight into the energetic demands of this species. Under standard laboratory conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the resting metabolic rate of adult Pseudoeurycea gadovii is 0.0015 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0015 milliliters of oxygen per hour], reflecting the low metabolic intensity typical of terrestrial plethodontid salamanders. This relatively modest rate of oxygen consumption aligns well with the species' secretive, low-activity lifestyle and its reliance on cutaneous respiration. Comparative data from congeneric species indicate that such metabolic economy is common among salamanders inhabiting cool, stable environments where energy expenditure must be carefully balanced against limited prey availability. The measurement was performed on post-absorptive individuals during their inactive phase to ensure true basal conditions, and repeated trials confirmed the consistency of this value across multiple subjects. These findings contribute to a broader understanding of how metabolic scaling relates to body size and thermal ecology within the Plethodontidae.

Body size parameters for Pseudoeurycea gadovii have been documented through long-term mark-recapture studies and examination of museum series. The ultimate wet weight attained by adults is 12.8 grams [Wwi = 12.8 grams], a body mass that places this species within the moderate size range for the genus. This asymptotic mass is reached gradually over several years of growth following metamorphosis, with individuals showing a pattern of slow but steady mass accumulation typical of long-lived, low-metabolic-rate amphibians. Females tend to achieve slightly larger body sizes than males, a common pattern in plethodontids that likely reflects the energetic demands of egg production. The maximum recorded longevity under natural conditions has been estimated at 18.5 years [am = 18.5 years] for individuals maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], an exceptionally long lifespan that underscores the species' slow life-history pace and delayed senescence. Such extended survival is consistent with the predictions of life-history theory for organisms inhabiting stable, low-productivity montane environments.

Reproductive output and maturation schedules have been characterized from both captive colonies and field populations. Females typically produce a single clutch of eggs per year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs per year], with each clutch containing approximately 100 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing approximately 100 eggs], yielding a maximum reproductive rate of 100 eggs per year when measured at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This annual fecundity is relatively modest compared to many pond-breeding amphibians but is typical of direct-developing and egg-laying plethodontids that invest heavily in yolk per offspring. The reproductive cycle appears tightly coupled to seasonal rainfall patterns, with oviposition concentrated during the wet season when soil moisture is highest and embryonic desiccation risk is minimized. Females reach sexual maturity at 1460 days following metamorphosis [tp = 1460 days following metamorphosis] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], indicating that approximately four years elapse between the completion of metamorphosis and the attainment of sexual maturity. This delayed maturation contributes to the species' characteristically slow generation time.

Comparative analyses of life-history traits across the Plethodontidae reveal that Pseudoeurycea gadovii occupies an extreme position along the slow-fast continuum. The combination of a small birth mass of 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], a substantial adult mass of 12.8 grams [Wwi = 12.8 grams], and a maximum longevity of 18.5 years [am = 18.5 years] yields a life-history profile that is heavily weighted toward late reproduction and high survival at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The extended prereproductive period, during which females require 1460 days following metamorphosis [tp = 1460 days following metamorphosis] to reach puberty, is consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by a low metabolic rate of 0.0015 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0015 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Annual reproductive output remains low at 100 eggs per year, but this modest fecundity is compensated by high adult survivorship and extended reproductive lifespan. Such demographic parameters suggest that populations of this species are particularly vulnerable to environmental perturbations that increase adult mortality.
